resources.string: The readings that have turned before past downturns.
Where cracks in the financial system show first.
Whether the country's borrowing is getting away from it.
What money costs, and what it's worth.

Normally lenders want more to lock money up for ten years than for two. When the 2-year pays more — an inverted curve — markets are betting the Fed will have to cut because a slowdown is coming. Every US recession since 1970 was preceded by one.
Below 0% the curve is inverted. Recessions have tended to arrive 6–24 months after inversion, often just as the curve turns positive again.
The New York Fed's preferred recession model uses this spread. It compares the 10-year yield with 3-month bills, which track the Fed's policy rate almost exactly.
Below 0% is inverted, the New York Fed model's strongest recession signal.
How far the 3-month average unemployment rate has risen above its low of the past year. Unemployment rarely rises a little: once it starts climbing it tends to keep going.
At 0.5 points the rule has called every recession since 1970, usually within months of it starting.
The share of people looking for work who can't find it. Jobs are what keep household spending — two thirds of the economy — going.
Above 5.5% layoffs are usually feeding on themselves.
New unemployment filings each week: the fastest hard data on layoffs, out every Thursday.
Sustained readings over 300k have marked every recession of the past 50 years.
How fast the economy grew last quarter after inflation, as an annual rate.
Two quarters in a row below zero is the textbook definition of a recession.
The University of Michigan's monthly survey of how people feel about their finances and the economy. Gloomy households stop spending.
Below 55 is the territory of 1980, 2008 and 2022.
The extra yield the riskiest companies pay over Treasuries. When lenders get scared of defaults this blows out, and companies that need to borrow can't.
Over 6% credit markets are pricing a wave of defaults (2008 peaked near 20%; March 2020 at 11%).
The St. Louis Fed's weekly blend of 18 market measures — rates, spreads, volatility. Zero is normal.
Above 1 the financial system is under real strain; 2008 hit 5.
Expected stock market volatility over the next 30 days, from options prices.
Above 30 the market is afraid; panics push it past 50.
The share of credit card balances at least 30 days late at US banks: how stretched households are.
Above 4.5% households are falling behind as they did going into 2008.
Everything the federal government owes, against a year of national output.
Over 125% the US is past its World War II peak (119% in 1946), and every rate rise lands on a bigger pile.
Interest as share of tax revenue
How much of every tax dollar goes to paying interest on the national debt. Money spent on interest can't be spent on anything else, and borrowing to pay it is how debt spirals start.
Above 30% the government spends more on interest than on almost anything else.
How fast the amount of money in the economy is growing. Booms run on it; it shrank for the first time since the 1930s in 2023.
Below 0% money is draining out of the economy — deflationary, and hard on borrowers.
How much prices rose over the past year, across everything a typical household buys.
Above 5% inflation is eating real incomes and forcing the Fed's hand.
Inflation without the swings of food and gas: the part that sticks.
The inflation measure the Federal Reserve actually targets at 2%.
The overnight rate the Federal Reserve sets. Every other interest rate in the country starts here.
Freddie Mac's weekly average 30-year fixed rate: what buying a house costs to finance.
Above 7.5% housing affordability is at its worst since the 1980s.
US home prices over the past year. Homes are most families' biggest asset; falling prices were the fuse in 2008.
Prices down 5% or more on a year ago means falling household wealth and underwater mortgages.
The rate the world's safest borrower pays for ten years, and the anchor for mortgages and corporate debt. A disorderly surge means buyers are demanding more to hold US debt.
Above 5.5% borrowing costs are at levels last seen before 2008.
Where markets expect the Fed's rate to be over the next two years.
The long bond: what investors want to lend to Washington for a generation.
